summary: Asked why His disciples do not fast, Jesus calls Himself the Bridegroom, foretells that He will be taken away, and speaks of new cloth and new wine.
key_insight: Jesus did not say fasting was wrong. He said it depended on who was present. While the Bridegroom was with them it was a wedding, not a funeral; “But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away.” In Mark, these are Jesus’ first words pointing to His death.
story: John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. {Mk} Then the disciples of John came to Jesus and asked, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but Your disciples do not fast?” {Mt} The Pharisees and their scribes, who had just complained about the company Jesus kept, pressed the same point: John’s disciples fasted often and made prayers, and so did the Pharisees’ disciples, “but Yours eat and drink?” {Lk}

Jesus answered with a picture from a wedding. “Can the friends of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them they cannot fast. But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” {Mk}

Then He spoke a parable to them. {Lk} No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, He said, or the new piece pulls away from the old, “and the tear is made worse.” {Mk} Nor does anyone cut a piece from a new garment to patch an old one; that ruins the new, and the patch does not match the old. {Lk}

“And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; or else the new wine bursts the wineskins, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined. But new wine must be put into new wineskins,” {Mk} “and both are preserved.” {Lk}
Then He added one more saying: “And no one, having drunk old wine, immediately desires new; for he says, ‘The old is better.’ ” {Lk}
differences: The questioners differ: in Matthew, John’s disciples ask; in Mark, “they came”; in Luke, the question continues the complaint of the Pharisees and their scribes at Levi’s feast.
Matthew has “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn”; Mark and Luke say “fast.” Mark alone adds, “As long as they have the bridegroom with them they cannot fast.”
Luke alone says John’s disciples “make prayers” and that Jesus’ disciples “eat and drink.” He also calls the sayings that follow a parable.
In Matthew and Mark the patch is unshrunk cloth on an old garment. In Luke it is a piece cut from a new garment, so both garments are spoiled.
Only Luke adds, “No one, having drunk old wine, immediately desires new.”

fit.question: Who asked the question? Matthew says John’s disciples came to Jesus. Mark says only that “they came.” Luke continues the conversation with the Pharisees and their scribes, who had complained at Levi’s feast (Luke 5:30).

points.label: Two groups, one complaint
points.text: Mark says both John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting, so both had reason to ask, and both may well have spoken. Matthew’s wording, “we and the Pharisees,” gives the question as John’s disciples put it. Luke’s wording, John’s disciples “and likewise those of the Pharisees,” sounds like the Pharisees’ side of the same challenge.

points.label: Mark’s open “they”
points.text: Mark’s phrase need not name anyone in particular; it can simply mean that people came and asked. He sets out who was fasting and lets the question stand for both groups.

fit.note: A question pressed by a mixed group is reported from where each writer stood. Nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: John’s disciples and the Pharisees were both fasting and both pressed the question. Matthew gives John’s disciples’ words; Luke gives the Pharisees’ side.

scene.label: John’s disciples
scene.text: John lived a severe life in the wilderness; Jesus later said, “John came neither eating nor drinking” (Matthew 11:18). By now John was in prison (Mark 1:14), and his disciples kept up his strict ways. Their question was probably sincere: why did Jesus, whom John had pointed to, not teach His men to do the same?

scene.label: A wedding week
scene.text: A wedding feast commonly lasted seven days (Genesis 29:27; Judges 14:12). The bridegroom’s friends were his companions and attendants through the celebration. Fasting, a sign of mourning, would have been out of place for the whole week.

scene.label: The Bridegroom
scene.text: The prophets pictured God as Israel’s husband and bridegroom: “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, So shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5; see Hosea 2:19). Jesus quietly takes that role for Himself.

scene.label: Unshrunk cloth
scene.text: New woven cloth had not yet been washed and shrunk. Sewn onto a worn garment as a patch, it would shrink at the first washing, pull at the weak old cloth around it and tear a bigger hole.

scene.label: Old wineskins
scene.text: Wine was stored in skins, usually goatskins sewn up whole. New wine was still fermenting and gave off gas. A new skin could stretch with it; an old skin, already stretched, dry and stiff, would split, and both the wine and the skin were lost.

witnesses.matthew: Gives the question in the words of John’s disciples and places it right after the meal with tax collectors and sinners, where Jesus had just quoted, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” Matthew alone has Jesus ask whether the bridegroom’s friends can “mourn,” which shows what fasting meant: grief.
witnesses.mark: Opens with the plain fact that both groups were fasting, and has Jesus say twice that the friends cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. This is the middle story of Mark’s five conflict stories (2:1–3:6), which end with a plot to destroy Him (3:6). At their center stands the Bridegroom who will be taken away.
witnesses.luke: Keeps the question at Levi’s feast, contrasts fasting and prayers with eating and drinking, and calls the sayings a parable. Luke alone adds the closing line about old wine, a gentle warning that those content with the old will not easily want the new.

seeing.reveals: Jesus calls Himself the Bridegroom, the role the prophets gave to God in His love for Israel. His presence made the season a wedding feast, and He already knew that He would be taken away.
seeing.living: Jesus did not abolish fasting; He said His followers would fast when He was taken away, and the early church did (Acts 13:2–3). Fasting now is longing for the absent Bridegroom, not a badge of seriousness. Ask whether your religious habits are ways of seeking Him, or old wineskins you have come to prefer to Him.
seeing.ponder: Are you more at home with the old wine of familiar religion than with the joy of Jesus Himself?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus brings a joy too new for old religious forms to hold.
outline: The Bridegroom present, then taken away (34–35)
The comfort of the old wine (39)
preaching.watch_for: Luke alone includes verse 39, and its quiet irony explains the scene. People who are content with old wine do not want to taste the new, and they say, “The old is better.” The critics are not short of evidence; they are attached to what they already have.
